name: Identity

subjectOf.text: Corruption is possible whenever actors in a governance design can be identified, and every historical instantiation of institutional governance design involving identifiable humans was afflicted by corruption sooner or later.
subjectOf.abstract: Corruption is possible if actors can be identified. Every instantiation of institutional governance design involving identifiable humans was afflicted by corruption sooner or later.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain-Based Corporate Governance (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3441904
scope_conditions: governance designs whose members are individually identifiable

subjectOf.text: The identity of actors in a DAO governance design typically creates corruptive elements, and merit identifiers other than individual identity remove the most corruptive influences.
subjectOf.abstract: Similarly, the identity of actors in a DAO governance design creates typically corruptive elements. Merit identifiers other than individual identity remove the most corruptive influences.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations – Internal Governance and External Legal Design (2020). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3652481

subjectOf.text: Equal distribution of output, where every member receives an equal share regardless of contribution, is impossible to maintain under current technology in a system with open access and privacy, because sockpuppet accounts would be abused.
subjectOf.abstract: This is impossible to maintain under the current technology with open access and privacy, since sockpuppet accounts would be abused. Improvements in ZK proofs and identity protocols, however, will soon make it possible to efficiently and securely com- bat such sockpuppet attacks.
subjectOf.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralized Governance (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782214

subjectOf.text: Superficial identifiers such as language, race, culture, social media profiles, and credit scores play less of a role in DAO of DAOs voting design, which allows inclusion of constituents who have no agency in centralized systems.
subjectOf.abstract: Such relatively superficial identifiers play less of a role in the DAO of DAOs voting designs. The more equal distribution of power in the DAO of DAOs governance design allows the inclusion of constituents who otherwise have no agency in centralized systems.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: reputation based voting rather than identity based access

subjectOf.text: Proof of personhood projects such as Proof of Humanity and UBI DAO fail because they rest on web-of-trust theory, which has been proven not to work long-term given the sockpuppet attacks that are inevitable in that design.
subjectOf.abstract: Of course, these attempts are all falling victim to web-of-trust theory that has been proven to not work long-term because the sockpuppet attacks that are inevitable in this design.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: identity systems built on web-of-trust vouching

subjectOf.text: Reputation systems that depend on persistent identity collapse in decentralized settings because agents can create new identities at no cost, so a poorly performing agent abandons its account and starts fresh, a practice known as whitewashing.
subjectOf.abstract: First, the identity problem: Reputation systems built on persistent identity5 collapse when agents can costlessly create new identities. A poorly-performing agent simply abandons their account and starts fresh, a phenomenon known as whitewashing.6
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Domain-Specific Reputation Systems From Binary Validation to Citation-Weighted Knowledge Attribution (2026). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=6192998
scope_conditions: decentralized or pseudonymous environments where identity creation is costless

subjectOf.text: Reputation in the underlying system is domain-specific and strictly non-transferable: bound to the holder's identity, earned only through validated work, and incapable of sale, loan or transfer.
subjectOf.abstract: Should intelligent agents have legal rights? This Article sets that question aside and asks a smaller one that matters more in practice. An intelligent agent that earns a reputation record has something to lose.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Should an Intelligent Agent Have Legal Rights? (2026). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=7596939

subjectOf.text: Copying an agent's weights confers no economic stake: a copy that does not continue the registered identity inherits no reputation and therefore no salary.

subjectOf.text: The Article resolves agent identity by legal stipulation rather than metaphysics: the legal subject is the registered record, continued by a recorded learning update within a prescribed granularity or by a recorded continuity transition, and only while the signing key stays within the registered configuration.
